# Standing army, pay and supply (`standing_army_logistics`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: helped by coinage, public_debt_bonds, census_vital_registration, paved_roads_macadam, canning
- Core idea: A permanent, regularly paid force that the state feeds, clothes and arms obeys in peace and war and can be drilled; an army that lives by plunder dissolves or turns on its employer. The arithmetic rules everything: a man needs about 1 kg of bread or grain a day, a horse about 10 kg of fodder, a wagon team eats its own load in a few weeks, so an army beyond a few days from a river, a port or stocked magazines must keep moving to fresh country or starve. Regular taxes, muster rolls that are actually checked, and depots laid out before the campaign are the invention, more than any weapon.
- Pitfalls:
  - Planning marches without counting fodder; animals, not men, are the larger part of the supply problem
  - Unpaid troops mutiny or sack friendly towns (Rome 1527, Antwerp 1576)
  - Muster rolls padded with dead or invented men unless inspected by someone who does not profit
  - A standing army is also a danger to the government that keeps it
  - Thinking armies could be supplied from home over long distances by cart before railways; water transport was the only bulk carrier
- History: mesopotamia: c. 745 BC – Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria creates a permanent royal army; china: 3rd c. BC – Qin and Han state arsenals, granaries and frontier garrisons; india: c. 300 BC – Mauryan standing army with a war office described by Megasthenes; rome: 107 BC – Marius enrols the propertyless (the scale of his 'reforms' is now disputed); 1st c. BC – long-service legions loyal to their generals; AD 6 – Augustus funds discharge pay from a military treasury; islamic: 14th c. – Ottoman Janissaries, paid standing infantry, with a road and depot system that carried the army to Vienna in 1683; europe: 1445 – French compagnies d'ordonnance; 1490 – Italian states still hire condottieri by contract; 1660s – magazines and intendants under Le Tellier and Louvois; americas: 15th c. – Inca storehouses (qollqa) and roads supply armies on the march
- Read:
  - Martin van Creveld, Supplying War: Logistics from Wallenstein to Patton (1977)
  - Donald W. Engels, Alexander the Great and the Logistics of the Macedonian Army (1978)
  - Jonathan P. Roth, The Logistics of the Roman Army at War (1999)
